name: Make charcoal
summary: Burn hardwood under restricted air until it stops smoking, then smother it — the feedstock for a filter, a hotter fire, and a wound-drawing poultice.

materials.item: metal container with a loose lid
soil or sand to smother with

steps.text: Pit method: burn a hot hardwood fire down in a pit until it is a bed of glowing coals with no flame.
Rake the coals level and cover them completely with 5-10 cm of soil, cutting off the air.
steps.why: Charcoal is what is left when wood is cooked without enough oxygen to finish burning. Air at this stage turns your charcoal into ash.

steps.text: Can method: pack hardwood into a metal can, put the lid on loose, and set it in the fire. Smoke and jets of flame will vent from the gap.
When the venting smoke stops, the wood has given up its volatiles. Pull the can out and seal the gap with soil.
Let it cool completely before opening — an hour or more. Opening it hot lets air in and it burns to ash.
Crush to coarse grit for a filter; keep lumps for fuel.

verify: Good charcoal is black through the break, light for its size, and rings faintly. Brown at the core means it was undercooked; grey and crumbling means it burned to ash.
It should snap cleanly rather than splinter like wood.
limits: This is charcoal, not ACTIVATED carbon. Activation needs steam or chemical treatment at temperatures a field fire does not hold, and the difference is roughly an order of magnitude in adsorptive surface.
Charcoal adsorbs some organics, tastes and odours. It does not remove pathogens, salt or most metals.
cautions: Only ever untreated wood. Painted, glued, pressure-treated or salvaged construction timber puts arsenic, formaldehyde and heavy metals into anything the charcoal later touches.
A smothered pit stays hot for many hours. Do not sleep on top of one.
